Direct chemical destruction of the epiglottic cartilage

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MCQ_Q44 - Directional gas gradients across alveolar membrane

questiontext.text: Consider the partial pressures of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) and \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) in alveoli (\(p\mathrm{O_2} = 104\text{ mm Hg}\), \(p\mathrm{CO_2} = 40\text{ mm Hg}\)) and systemic deoxygenated blood (\(p\mathrm{O_2} = 40\text{ mm Hg}\), \(p\mathrm{CO_2} = 45\text{ mm Hg}\)). The resulting concentration gradients drive:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Calculate the pressure gradient for oxygen.
Alveolar \(p\mathrm{O_2}\) (\(104\text{ mm Hg}\)) is higher than blood \(p\mathrm{O_2}\) (\(40\text{ mm Hg}\)), driving \(\mathrm{O_2}\) from alveoli into blood.

Step 2: Calculate the pressure gradient for carbon dioxide.
Deoxygenated blood \(p\mathrm{CO_2}\) (\(45\text{ mm Hg}\)) exceeds alveolar \(p\mathrm{CO_2}\) (\(40\text{ mm Hg}\)), driving \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) from blood into alveoli.

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
Diffusion of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) occurs from alveoli to blood and diffusion of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) occurs from blood to alveoli.

answer.text: \(\mathrm{O_2}\) from alveoli into blood and \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) from blood into alveoli
\(\mathrm{CO_2}\) from alveoli into blood and \(\mathrm{O_2}\) from blood into alveoli
Both \(\mathrm{O_2}\) and \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) from alveoli into blood
Both \(\mathrm{O_2}\) and \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) from blood into alveoli

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MCQ_Q45 - Role of epiglottis during deglutition

questiontext.text: During the process of swallowing, entry of food into the larynx is prevented by the closure of the glottis by which structure?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the anatomical opening to the airway.
The glottis is the opening of the larynx.

Step 2: Identify the protective cartilaginous flap.
A thin, elastic cartilaginous flap called the epiglottis folds over the glottis during swallowing to divert food into the oesophagus.

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
The glottis is covered by the epiglottis.

answer.text: A thin elastic cartilaginous flap called epiglottis
The thyroid cartilage
The soft palate alone
The cricoid cartilage

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MCQ_Q46 - Bicarbonate dissociation at alveolar interface

questiontext.text: When bicarbonate-rich blood arrives at the pulmonary capillaries where \(p\mathrm{CO_2}\) is low, carbonic anhydrase facilitates the formation of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Examine the chemical equilibrium of carbonic anhydrase.
\(\mathrm{CO_2} + \mathrm{H_2O} \xrightleftharpoons{} \mathrm{H_2CO_3} \xrightleftharpoons{} \mathrm{HCO_3^-} + \mathrm{H^+}\).

Step 2: Determine reaction direction at low \(p\mathrm{CO_2}\).
At the alveolar site where \(p\mathrm{CO_2}\) is low, the equilibrium shifts to the left: \(\mathrm{HCO_3^-}\) and \(\mathrm{H^+}\) combine to form carbonic acid, which rapidly cleaves into \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) and \(\mathrm{H_2O}\).

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
The reaction leads to the release of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) and \(\mathrm{H_2O}\).

answer.text: \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) and \(\mathrm{H_2O}\)
\(\mathrm{H_2CO_3}\) precipitate only
Carbamino-haemoglobin directly
Carbon monoxide and oxygen

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MCQ_Q47 - Right shift of oxygen dissociation curve

questiontext.text: A rightward shift of the oxygen dissociation curve of haemoglobin signifies a decreased affinity for oxygen. Which condition causes this rightward shift?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand what causes a right shift in the oxygen dissociation curve.
A rightward shift indicates that a higher \(p\mathrm{O_2}\) is required to achieve 50% saturation, meaning oxygen affinity is reduced (Bohr effect).

Step 2: Identify allosteric factors promoting right shift.
Increased \(p\mathrm{CO_2}\), increased \(\mathrm{H^+}\) concentration (decreased pH), elevated temperature, and increased 2,3-BPG promote right shift and oxygen release.

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
High \(p\mathrm{CO_2}\) and high \(\mathrm{H^+}\) concentration shift the curve to the right.

answer.text: High \(p\mathrm{CO_2}\) and high \(\mathrm{H^+}\) concentration
Low \(p\mathrm{CO_2}\) and low \(\mathrm{H^+}\) concentration
Low temperature and high arterial \(p\mathrm{O_2}\)
Alkaline pH and decreased \(\mathrm{CO_2}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MCQ_Q48 - Pleural membrane layers and fluid function

questiontext.text: The human lungs are enclosed by a double-layered pleura with pleural fluid between them. Which statement correctly identifies the anatomical relationship of these layers?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the two layers of the pleura.
The lungs are surrounded by an outer parietal pleural membrane and an inner visceral pleural membrane.

Step 2: Describe their specific contacts and fluid role.
The outer pleural membrane remains in close contact with the thoracic lining, whereas the inner pleural membrane is in intimate contact with the lung surface. Pleural fluid between them reduces friction during respiratory excursions.

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
The outer pleura contacts the thoracic lining and the inner pleura contacts the lung surface.

answer.text: The outer pleural membrane is in contact with the thoracic lining, whereas the inner pleural membrane contacts the lung surface
The inner pleural membrane is in contact with the ribs, whereas the outer membrane contacts the alveolar basement
Both pleural membranes directly adhere to the pericardium without enclosing fluid
The outer pleural membrane lines the tracheal cartilages while the inner membrane lines the sternum

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHING_AND_EXCHANGE_OF_GASES_STATEMENT_Q01 - Respiratory organs across different animal groups

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Lower invertebrates like sponges, coelenterates, and flatworms exchange \( \mathrm{O}_2 \) with \( \mathrm{CO}_2 \) by simple diffusion over their entire body surface.

Statement II: Aquatic arthropods and molluscs use vascularised bags called lungs for the exchange of respiratory gases.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle.
Mechanisms of breathing in the animal kingdom depend primarily on their habitats and levels of structural organisation. Simple body plans utilize direct diffusion, whereas specialized organs evolve in complex metazoans.

Step 2: Evaluation of the first claim.
Lower invertebrates such as sponges, coelenterates, and flatworms lack specialised respiratory organs; they exchange \( \mathrm{O}_2 \) with \( \mathrm{CO}_2 \) by simple diffusion over their entire body surface. Hence, the first claim is biologically accurate.

Step 3: Evaluation of the second claim.
Aquatic arthropods and molluscs utilize special vascularised structures called gills for branchial respiration. In contrast, vascularised bags called lungs (pulmonary respiration) are adapted for terrestrial forms. Thus, the second claim is inaccurate.

Step 4: Final Conclusion.
The statement describing simple diffusion across the body surface in lower invertebrates is correct, whereas the statement claiming lungs are used by aquatic arthropods and molluscs is incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHING_AND_EXCHANGE_OF_GASES_STATEMENT_Q02 - Conducting versus exchange parts of respiratory system

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The conducting part of the human respiratory system represents the site of actual diffusion of \( \mathrm{O}_2 \) and \( \mathrm{CO}_2 \) between blood and atmospheric air.

Statement II: The conducting part transports atmospheric air to the alveoli, clears it from foreign particles, humidifies it, and brings it to body temperature.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle.
The human respiratory tract is anatomically and functionally divided into two distinct regions: the conducting zone (from external nostrils to terminal bronchioles) and the respiratory/exchange zone (alveoli and their ducts).

Step 2: Evaluation of the first claim.
The exchange part, consisting of alveoli and their ducts, is the actual site of diffusion of \( \mathrm{O}_2 \) and \( \mathrm{CO}_2 \) between blood and alveolar air. The conducting part does not participate in gas diffusion. Therefore, the first claim is incorrect.

Step 3: Evaluation of the second claim.
The conducting part carries out air conditioning functions: it transports atmospheric air to the alveoli, clears it of particulate matter via mucus and cilia, humidifies the incoming air, and thermalizes it to normal body temperature. Therefore, the second claim is correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion.
The statement designating the conducting zone as the site of gas diffusion is incorrect, whereas the statement outlining the protective and conditioning functions of the conducting zone is correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHING_AND_EXCHANGE_OF_GASES_STATEMENT_Q03 - Anatomical boundaries of the human thoracic chamber

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The thoracic chamber is anatomically an air-tight chamber formed dorsally by the vertebral column and ventrally by the sternum.

Statement II: The thoracic chamber is bounded laterally by the ribs and on the lower side by the dome-shaped diaphragm.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle.
The lungs sit inside an anatomically sealed, air-tight thoracic chamber. This structural setup ensures that any change in thoracic volume directly alters pulmonary volume, which is essential for pulmonary ventilation.

Step 2: Evaluation of the dorsal and ventral boundaries.
The dorsal wall of the thoracic cage is constructed by the vertebral column, while the ventral anterior wall is supported by the flat sternum. Thus, the first statement accurately describes these anatomical boundaries.

Step 3: Evaluation of the lateral and inferior boundaries.
The lateral walls of the thoracic cavity are formed by the curving ribs, and the base (inferior margin) is closed off by the muscular, dome-shaped diaphragm. Thus, the second statement is also factually correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion.
Both assertions regarding the anatomical boundaries that enclose the air-tight thoracic cavity are completely correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHING_AND_EXCHANGE_OF_GASES_STATEMENT_Q04 - Muscular mechanisms and axes of thoracic expansion

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Contraction of the diaphragm increases the volume of the thoracic chamber in the dorso-ventral axis.

Statement II: Contraction of the external intercostal muscles lifts up the ribs and sternum, causing an increase in the volume of the thoracic chamber in the antero-posterior axis.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle.
Inspiration is an active process requiring thoracic volume expansion along two perpendicular anatomical axes: antero-posterior and dorso-ventral.

Step 2: Evaluation of the diaphragm action.
Contraction of the dome-shaped diaphragm flattens it downward toward the abdomen, which increases the thoracic volume along the antero-posterior (longitudinal) axis, not the dorso-ventral axis. Hence, the first claim is incorrect.

Step 3: Evaluation of external intercostal action.
Contraction of external intercostal muscles pulls the ribs and sternum upward and outward, expanding the ribcage in the dorso-ventral axis, not the antero-posterior axis. Hence, the second claim is also incorrect.

Step 4: Final Conclusion.
Both statements have inverted the respective axes of thoracic expansion and are therefore incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHING_AND_EXCHANGE_OF_GASES_STATEMENT_Q05 - Normal respiratory rate and role of abdominal muscles

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: On an average, a healthy human breathes \( 12\text{--}16 \) times per minute under resting conditions.

Statement II: Humans possess the ability to increase the strength of both inspiration and expiration with the help of additional muscles in the abdomen.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle.
Normal resting ventilation is maintained by rhythmic passive and active cycles, but during increased metabolic demands or forced breathing, accessory musculature is recruited.

Step 2: Evaluation of the resting respiratory frequency.
Under basal resting conditions, the physiological breathing rate of a healthy adult human averages \( 12\text{ to }16\text{ breaths/min} \). Therefore, the first statement is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the role of abdominal musculature.
Contraction of anterior abdominal wall muscles compresses the abdominal viscera, pushing the diaphragm upward and depressing the lower ribs, thereby aiding forceful expiration and increasing respiratory vigor. Thus, the second statement is correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion.
Both statements regarding respiratory frequency and the recruitment of abdominal muscles during forced ventilation are fully correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHING_AND_EXCHANGE_OF_GASES_STATEMENT_Q06 - Tidal volume and inspiratory reserve volume values

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV) is the additional volume of air a person can inspire by forcible inspiration, averaging \( 1000\text{ mL to }1100\text{ mL} \).

Statement II: A healthy adult human can inspire or expire approximately \( 6000\text{ to }8000\text{ mL} \) of air per minute during normal quiet breathing.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Definitions.
Tidal volume \( (\mathrm{TV}) \approx 500\text{ mL} \); normal respiratory rate \( = 12\text{--}16\text{ breaths/min} \); Expiratory Reserve Volume \( (\mathrm{ERV}) = 1000\text{--}1100\text{ mL} \); Inspiratory Reserve Volume \( (\mathrm{IRV}) = 2500\text{--}3000\text{ mL} \).

Step 2: Evaluation of the claim on Inspiratory Reserve Volume.
The volume of air a person can inspire beyond normal tidal volume by forced effort averages \( 2500\text{ to }3000\text{ mL} \). The range \( 1000\text{ to }1100\text{ mL} \) corresponds to the Expiratory Reserve Volume \( (\mathrm{ERV}) \). Hence, the first claim is incorrect.

Step 3: Evaluation of minute respiratory volume.
Minute volume is calculated as \( \mathrm{TV} \times \text{breathing rate} = 500\text{ mL} \times (12\text{ to }16) = 6000\text{ to }8000\text{ mL/min} \). Hence, the second claim is correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion.
The statement stating IRV is \( 1000\text{--}1100\text{ mL} \) is incorrect, whereas the statement providing the minute ventilation volume is correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHING_AND_EXCHANGE_OF_GASES_STATEMENT_Q07 - Components of functional residual capacity and vital capacity

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) is the volume of air that remains in the lungs after a normal expiration and is equal to \( \mathrm{ERV} + \mathrm{RV} \).

Statement II: Vital Capacity (VC) is the maximum volume of air a person can breathe in after a forced expiration and includes \( \mathrm{ERV} + \mathrm{TV} + \mathrm{IRV} + \mathrm{RV} \).

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Relevant Formulae and Principles.
\( \mathrm{FRC} = \mathrm{ERV} + \mathrm{RV} \)
\( \mathrm{VC} = \mathrm{ERV} + \mathrm{TV} + \mathrm{IRV} \)
\( \mathrm{TLC} = \mathrm{VC} + \mathrm{RV} = \mathrm{ERV} + \mathrm{TV} + \mathrm{IRV} + \mathrm{RV} \)

Step 2: Evaluation of Functional Residual Capacity.
Functional Residual Capacity represents the volume of air remaining in the lungs after the passive, unforced outflow of a normal expiration. It consists of the expiratory reserve volume plus the residual volume (\( \mathrm{ERV} + \mathrm{RV} \)). Hence, this assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of Vital Capacity.
Vital Capacity represents the maximum exchangeable volume of gas: \( \mathrm{VC} = \mathrm{ERV} + \mathrm{TV} + \mathrm{IRV} \). It explicitly excludes the non-expellable Residual Volume (\( \mathrm{RV} \)). The sum that includes \( \mathrm{RV} \) defines Total Lung Capacity (\( \mathrm{TLC} \)). Hence, this assertion is incorrect.

Step 4: Final Conclusion.
The statement defining FRC as \( \mathrm{ERV} + \mathrm{RV} \) is correct, whereas the statement defining VC with the inclusion of RV is incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHING_AND_EXCHANGE_OF_GASES_STATEMENT_Q08 - Partial pressures of respiratory gases across diffusion sites

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The partial pressure of carbon dioxide (\( \mathrm{pCO}_2 \)) in oxygenated blood is \( 45\text{ mm Hg} \), which matches the partial pressure found in metabolising tissues.

Statement II: The partial pressure of oxygen (\( \mathrm{pO}_2 \)) in alveolar air is \( 104\text{ mm Hg} \), which establishes a concentration gradient towards deoxygenated pulmonary capillary blood.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Physiological Values.
Alveoli: \( \mathrm{pO}_2 = 104\text{ mm Hg} \), \( \mathrm{pCO}_2 = 40\text{ mm Hg} \).
Deoxygenated blood: \( \mathrm{pO}_2 = 40\text{ mm Hg} \), \( \mathrm{pCO}_2 = 45\text{ mm Hg} \).
Oxygenated blood: \( \mathrm{pO}_2 = 95\text{ mm Hg} \), \( \mathrm{pCO}_2 = 40\text{ mm Hg} \).
Tissues: \( \mathrm{pO}_2 = 40\text{ mm Hg} \), \( \mathrm{pCO}_2 = 45\text{ mm Hg} \).

Step 2: Evaluation of the claim regarding oxygenated blood \( \mathrm{pCO}_2 \).
The partial pressure of \( \mathrm{CO}_2 \) in oxygenated blood is \( 40\text{ mm Hg} \), not \( 45\text{ mm Hg} \). In tissues and deoxygenated blood, \( \mathrm{pCO}_2 \) is \( 45\text{ mm Hg} \). Therefore, the first statement is incorrect.

Step 3: Evaluation of the claim regarding alveolar \( \mathrm{pO}_2 \).
The alveolar \( \mathrm{pO}_2 \) of \( 104\text{ mm Hg} \) is markedly higher than the \( 40\text{ mm Hg} \) present in deoxygenated blood arriving at pulmonary capillaries, driving net diffusion of \( \mathrm{O}_2 \) into the blood. Therefore, the second statement is correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion.
The statement assigning \( 45\text{ mm Hg} \) to \( \mathrm{pCO}_2 \) in oxygenated blood is incorrect, whereas the statement detailing alveolar \( \mathrm{pO}_2 \) and its gradient is correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHING_AND_EXCHANGE_OF_GASES_STATEMENT_Q09 - Solubility and diffusion rates of respiratory gases

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The solubility of \( \mathrm{CO}_2 \) in aqueous and biological fluids is \( 20\text{ to }25 \) times higher than that of \( \mathrm{O}_2 \).

Statement II: The amount of \( \mathrm{CO}_2 \) that can diffuse across the respiratory membrane per unit difference in partial pressure is substantially greater than that of \( \mathrm{O}_2 \).

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Physical Principles of Gas Diffusion.
According to Fick's law of diffusion, the rate of net gas transfer across a biological membrane is directly proportional to the gas solubility and partial pressure difference, and inversely proportional to membrane thickness.

Step 2: Evaluation of the relative solubility.
Carbon dioxide possesses a chemical solubility in liquid media that is \( 20\text{--}25 \) times higher than that of oxygen. Thus, the first statement is biologically and physically correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of diffusion capacity per unit partial pressure.
Because \( \mathrm{CO}_2 \) is significantly more soluble than \( \mathrm{O}_2 \), a much smaller partial pressure gradient (\( 45 - 40 = 5\text{ mm Hg} \)) suffices to diffuse equivalent amounts of \( \mathrm{CO}_2 \) compared to the large gradient required for \( \mathrm{O}_2 \) (\( 104 - 40 = 64\text{ mm Hg} \)). Thus, the second statement is correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion.
Both statements regarding the high solubility of carbon dioxide and its resulting high diffusion rate per unit pressure difference are correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHING_AND_EXCHANGE_OF_GASES_STATEMENT_Q10 - Layers and total thickness of diffusion membrane

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The diffusion membrane across which alveolar exchange occurs is composed of three major layers: the thin squamous epithelium of alveoli, the endothelium of alveolar capillaries, and the intervening basement substance.

Statement II: The total thickness of the diffusion membrane in human lungs is slightly greater than two millimetres to provide mechanical resistance.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Histological Structure of the Alveolar-Capillary Barrier.
The respiratory barrier consists of: (1) single-layered squamous alveolar epithelium, (2) single-layered endothelial wall of the pulmonary capillary, and (3) an acellular basement substance supporting them.

Step 2: Evaluation of the layer composition.
The three microscopic components forming the barrier are precisely the alveolar squamous epithelium, the capillary endothelium, and the fused basement substance. Therefore, the first claim is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the membrane thickness.
To facilitate rapid diffusion without offering significant resistance, the total thickness of this tripartite membrane is extremely small, being much less than a millimetre (typically \( < 0.5\text{ }\mu\mathrm{m} \)). A thickness of two millimetres would virtually abolish gas exchange. Therefore, the second claim is incorrect.

Step 4: Final Conclusion.
The statement identifying the three constituent histological layers is correct, but the statement asserting its thickness is greater than two millimetres is incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHING_AND_EXCHANGE_OF_GASES_STATEMENT_Q11 - Transport forms and percentages of blood oxygen

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: About \( 97 \) per cent of oxygen is transported in the blood bound to haemoglobin inside red blood cells.

Statement II: The remaining \( 3 \) per cent of oxygen is carried in a dissolved physical state through blood plasma.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle.
Oxygen possesses low solubility in aqueous solutions. Consequently, simple physical dissolution in plasma cannot fulfill vertebrate metabolic requirements, necessitating an iron-containing metalloprotein carrier (haemoglobin).

Step 2: Evaluation of the intra-erythrocytic transport percentage.
Approximately \( 97\% \) of all oxygen in systemic arterial blood is bound chemically to haemoglobin inside erythrocytes as oxyhaemoglobin. Hence, the first claim is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the dissolved transport percentage.
Because of its low Henry's law solubility coefficient in water, only about \( 3\% \) of circulating oxygen travels physically dissolved in the plasma water. Hence, the second claim is correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion.
Both statements accurately describe the quantitative distribution of oxygen transported in erythrocytes and blood plasma.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHING_AND_EXCHANGE_OF_GASES_STATEMENT_Q12 - Physiological gas delivery volumes by circulating blood

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Under normal physiological conditions, every \( 100\text{ mL} \) of oxygenated blood delivers around \( 15\text{ mL} \) of \( \mathrm{O}_2 \) to the peripheral tissues.

Statement II: Every \( 100\text{ mL} \) of deoxygenated blood delivers approximately \( 40\text{ mL} \) of \( \mathrm{CO}_2 \) to the pulmonary alveoli.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Quantitative Gas Exchange Values.
Oxygenated blood leaves the lungs with approximately \( 20\text{ mL of }\mathrm{O}_2\text{ per }100\text{ mL} \) of blood. At rest, venous blood retains approximately \( 15\text{ mL of }\mathrm{O}_2\text{ per }100\text{ mL} \), releasing \( 5\text{ mL of }\mathrm{O}_2 \) to the tissues.

Step 2: Evaluation of the oxygen delivery claim.
Under basal resting conditions, each \( 100\text{ mL} \) of oxygenated blood unloads around \( 5\text{ mL} \) of \( \mathrm{O}_2 \) to body tissues, not \( 15\text{ mL} \). Therefore, the first statement is incorrect.

Step 3: Evaluation of the carbon dioxide delivery claim.
Every \( 100\text{ mL} \) of venous (deoxygenated) blood delivers approximately \( 4\text{ mL} \) of \( \mathrm{CO}_2 \) into the alveolar air spaces for expiration, not \( 40\text{ mL} \). Therefore, the second statement is incorrect.

Step 4: Final Conclusion.
Both statements overestimate the physiological delivery quantities of oxygen and carbon dioxide by a factor of three and ten respectively, making both statements incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHING_AND_EXCHANGE_OF_GASES_STATEMENT_Q13 - Factors regulating formation and dissociation of oxyhaemoglobin

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In the pulmonary alveoli, high \( \mathrm{pO}_2 \), low \( \mathrm{pCO}_2 \), lesser \( \mathrm{H}^+ \) concentration, and lower temperature favour the binding of oxygen to haemoglobin.

Statement II: In metabolising tissues, low \( \mathrm{pO}_2 \), high \( \mathrm{pCO}_2 \), high \( \mathrm{H}^+ \) concentration, and higher temperature promote the dissociation of oxygen from oxyhaemoglobin.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle.
The sigmoidal oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve reflects allosteric cooperative binding influenced by microenvironmental conditions (Bohr effect and thermal effects).

Step 2: Evaluation of the alveolar environment.
At the respiratory surface of alveoli, alveolar air has high \( \mathrm{pO}_2 \) (\( 104\text{ mm Hg} \)), low \( \mathrm{pCO}_2 \) (\( 40\text{ mm Hg} \)), low acidity (lesser \( \mathrm{H}^+ \) concentration / higher pH), and lower temperature. These conditions shift the curve leftward, maximizing oxyhaemoglobin synthesis. Hence, the first assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the tissue environment.
Metabolically active cells consume \( \mathrm{O}_2 \) and generate \( \mathrm{CO}_2 \), lactic acid, and heat, creating a microenvironment characterized by low \( \mathrm{pO}_2 \), high \( \mathrm{pCO}_2 \), high \( \mathrm{H}^+ \) concentration, and elevated temperature. These factors shift the dissociation curve rightward, promoting \( \mathrm{O}_2 \) unloading. Hence, the second assertion is correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion.
Both statements regarding the local biochemical conditions promoting loading at the lungs and unloading at the tissues are fully correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHING_AND_EXCHANGE_OF_GASES_STATEMENT_Q14 - Bicarbonate transport and distribution of carbonic anhydrase

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The zinc-containing enzyme carbonic anhydrase is present in high concentration in red blood cells and is completely absent in blood plasma.

Statement II: Nearly \( 70 \) per cent of carbon dioxide is transported from tissues to lungs in the form of bicarbonate ions (\( \mathrm{HCO}_3^- \)).

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Chemical Mechanisms of \( \mathrm{CO}_2 \) Transport.
Carbon dioxide is transported in three ways: dissolved in plasma (\( \sim 7\% \)), as carbamino-haemoglobin (\( 20\text{--}25\% \)), and as bicarbonate ions (\( \sim 70\% \)).

Step 2: Evaluation of the claim on enzyme distribution.
Erythrocytes contain an exceptionally high concentration of carbonic anhydrase, but minute quantities of this enzyme are also present in the blood plasma. It is not completely absent in plasma. Therefore, the first statement is incorrect.

Step 3: Evaluation of bicarbonate transport percentage.
The primary mode of carbon dioxide transport is indeed in the form of bicarbonate ions (\( \mathrm{HCO}_3^- \)), which accounts for approximately \( 70\% \) of total carbon dioxide transported. Therefore, the second statement is correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion.
The statement stating that carbonic anhydrase is entirely absent in plasma is incorrect, whereas the statement noting that about 70 percent of carbon dioxide travels as bicarbonate is correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHING_AND_EXCHANGE_OF_GASES_STATEMENT_Q15 - Neural regulation of rhythm and chemical receptors

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: A centre present in the pons region of the brain called the pneumotaxic centre can moderate the functions of the medullary respiratory rhythm centre.

Statement II: The role of oxygen in the normal regulation of respiratory rhythm is quite insignificant compared to that of carbon dioxide and hydrogen ions.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Neuro-Anatomy of Respiratory Centers.
The primary pacemaker for ventilation is the respiratory rhythm centre located in the medulla oblongata. A secondary moderating area, the pneumotaxic centre, resides in the pons.

Step 2: Evaluation of the pneumotaxic centre function.
Neural signals from the pontine pneumotaxic centre limit the duration of inspiration (acting as an "off-switch" for the inspiratory ramp), thereby modulating respiratory depth and rate. Hence, the first statement is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of chemical chemoreceptor sensitivity.
Central chemosensitive areas and peripheral chemoreceptors in the aortic arch and carotid bodies are exquisitely tuned to increases in \( \mathrm{CO}_2 \) and \( \mathrm{H}^+ \) concentrations. Under physiological resting conditions, arterial \( \mathrm{pO}_2 \) plays an insignificant role in regulating respiratory rhythm. Hence, the second statement is correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion.
Both statements regarding the regulatory role of the pneumotaxic centre and the insignificant role of oxygen in standard rhythm regulation are correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHING_AND_EXCHANGE_OF_GASES_STATEMENT_Q16 - Distinct clinical features of asthma and emphysema

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Asthma is a chronic disorder in which alveolar walls are damaged, resulting in a persistent reduction of the respiratory surface.

Statement II: Emphysema is characterized by difficulty in breathing causing wheezing due to acute inflammation of the bronchi and bronchioles.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Pathophysiological Definitions.
Asthma and emphysema are two common obstructive pulmonary conditions with differing pathophysiological lesions.

Step 2: Evaluation of the description of Asthma.
Asthma is characterized by episodic difficulty in breathing and wheezing caused by hyper-reactivity and inflammation of the bronchi and bronchioles, not the destruction of alveolar walls. Therefore, the first statement is incorrect.

Step 3: Evaluation of the description of Emphysema.
Emphysema is a chronic pulmonary disease, commonly triggered by cigarette smoking, in which the alveolar septal walls undergo irreversible breakdown, drastically reducing total surface area available for diffusion. It is not defined as inflammation of bronchi/bronchioles. Therefore, the second statement is incorrect.

Step 4: Final Conclusion.
Because the clinical and histological descriptions of asthma and emphysema have been transposed, both statements are incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER14_STATEMENT3_Q01 - Diversity of respiratory mechanisms across animal taxa

questiontext.text:
Identify whether the following statements are correct or incorrect:

Statement I: Lower invertebrates such as sponges, coelenterates, and flatworms exchange oxygen with carbon dioxide by simple diffusion over their entire body surface.

Statement II: Earthworms utilise their moist cuticle for respiration, whereas insects possess a tracheal network of tubes to transport atmospheric air within the body.

Statement III: Gills are vascularised structures utilised exclusively by terrestrial molluscs, whereas lungs are used solely by aquatic arthropods.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Mechanisms of respiration across animal taxa depend heavily on their natural habitats and structural levels of organisation. Gas exchange can occur via general body surface diffusion, moist cuticle, specialized tracheal systems, branchial structures (gills), or vascularised bags (pulmonary lungs).

Step 2: Evaluation of First Proposition
Organisms with simple body plans like sponges, cnidarians, and flatworms lack specialized circulatory and respiratory organs; gas exchange takes place readily via simple diffusion across their outer body surfaces.

Step 3: Evaluation of Second Proposition
Annelids such as earthworms exhibit cutaneous respiration using their moist outer cuticle, while terrestrial arthropods like insects use an internal branching system of tracheal tubes to directly convey atmospheric air to body tissues.

Step 4: Evaluation of Third Proposition
Gills (branchial respiration) are specialized vascularised organs adapted for aquatic respiration, commonly employed by aquatic molluscs and aquatic arthropods. Conversely, lungs (pulmonary respiration) are vascularised sacs evolved in terrestrial forms for gas exchange in air.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The assertions concerning general surface diffusion in lower invertebrates and the mechanisms in earthworms and insects are factual, whereas the assertion reversing the roles of gills and lungs in molluscs and arthropods is false.

answer.text: Statements I and II are correct, but Statement III is incorrect
Statements I and III are correct, but Statement II is incorrect
Statements II and III are correct, but Statement I is incorrect
Statements I, II and III are all correct

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER14_STATEMENT3_Q02 - Anatomical division of trachea and bronchial tree

questiontext.text:
Identify whether the following statements are correct or incorrect:

Statement I: The trachea is a straight tube extending up to the mid-thoracic cavity, which bifurcates at the level of the 5th thoracic vertebra into right and left primary bronchi.

Statement II: Incomplete cartilaginous rings support the trachea, primary, secondary, and tertiary bronchi, as well as the initial bronchioles.

Statement III: The terminal bronchioles give rise to thin, irregular-walled, vascularised bag-like structures called alveoli, which are also reinforced by complete cartilaginous rings.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The human respiratory tract begins at the external nostrils and leads through the pharynx, larynx, trachea, and branching bronchial tree down to terminal bronchioles and alveolar structures. Cartilaginous support prevents collapse during changes in airway pressure.

Step 2: Evaluation of First Proposition
The trachea runs through the neck into the mid-thoracic cavity and specifically divides at the level of the fifth thoracic vertebra into the primary bronchi heading toward the two lungs.

Step 3: Evaluation of Second Proposition
Structural rigidity and patency of the conducting airways are maintained by C-shaped incomplete cartilaginous rings that extend along the trachea, primary, secondary, and tertiary bronchi, ending at the initial bronchioles.

Step 4: Evaluation of Third Proposition
Terminal bronchioles branch into respiratory ducts and thin, vascularised irregular-walled sacs known as alveoli. Alveoli and their alveolar ducts lack any cartilaginous rings, allowing extremely thin barriers for efficient diffusion of respiratory gases.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The propositions describing tracheal bifurcation at the fifth thoracic vertebra and cartilaginous support through initial bronchioles are accurate, whereas the assertion that alveoli have complete cartilaginous rings is inaccurate.

answer.text: Statements I and II are correct, but Statement III is incorrect
Statements I and III are correct, but Statement II is incorrect
Statements II and III are correct, but Statement I is incorrect
Statements I, II and III are all correct

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER14_STATEMENT3_Q03 - Pleural anatomy and thoracic chamber boundaries

questiontext.text:
Identify whether the following statements are correct or incorrect:

Statement I: The lungs are enclosed by a double-layered pleura, wherein the outer pleural membrane is in close contact with the thoracic lining and the inner pleural membrane is in contact with the lung surface.

Statement II: Pleural fluid situated between the two pleural membranes increases friction on the lung surface during continuous breathing movements.

Statement III: The thoracic chamber is anatomically an air-tight chamber formed dorsally by the vertebral column, ventrally by the sternum, laterally by the ribs, and on the lower side by the dome-shaped diaphragm.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The mechanics of pulmonary ventilation require an air-tight thoracic cage and a lubricated pleural cavity to ensure that thoracic volume fluctuations faithfully translate into pulmonary volume alterations.

Step 2: Evaluation of First Proposition
The lungs are encased by two continuous serous pleural layers: the outer parietal pleura adhering to the thoracic wall lining and the inner visceral pleura directly adhering to the lung tissue.

Step 3: Evaluation of Second Proposition
The thin film of pleural fluid between the parietal and visceral layers serves as a lubricant that reduces friction during respiratory expansion and recoil, rather than increasing it.

Step 4: Evaluation of Third Proposition
The thoracic cage is anatomically defined by the vertebral column on the dorsal aspect, the sternum ventrally, the ribs laterally, and the muscular diaphragm inferiorly, forming a closed air-tight system.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The descriptions of pleural membrane placement and thoracic chamber boundaries are scientifically correct, whereas the statement attributing increased friction to pleural fluid is incorrect.

answer.text: Statements I and III are correct, but Statement II is incorrect
Statements I and II are correct, but Statement III is incorrect
Statements II and III are correct, but Statement I is incorrect
Statements I, II and III are all correct

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER14_STATEMENT3_Q04 - Muscular mechanism and pressure changes in inspiration

questiontext.text:
Identify whether the following statements are correct or incorrect:

Statement I: Inspiration is initiated by the contraction of the diaphragm, which increases the volume of the thoracic chamber in the antero-posterior axis.

Statement II: Contraction of the external intercostal muscles lifts the ribs and sternum, causing an increase in the volume of the thoracic chamber in the dorso-ventral axis.

Statement III: An overall increase in thoracic volume increases the intra-pulmonary pressure above atmospheric pressure, driving air into the lungs.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Air moves down pressure gradients into and out of the lungs. Boyle's law governs the relationship between pulmonary volume and intra-pulmonary pressure: an increase in volume produces a decrease in pressure relative to the atmosphere.

Step 2: Evaluation of First Proposition
When the dome-shaped diaphragm contracts, it flattens downward toward the abdominal cavity, thereby expanding thoracic volume along the antero-posterior axis.

Step 3: Evaluation of Second Proposition
Simultaneous contraction of the external intercostal muscles elevates the ribs and moves the sternum outward, which enlarges the thoracic cage along the dorso-ventral axis.

Step 4: Evaluation of Third Proposition
Expansion of thoracic volume causes an identical increase in pulmonary volume, which drops intra-pulmonary pressure below atmospheric pressure (creating negative intra-pulmonary pressure), causing atmospheric air to flow into the lungs. An intra-pulmonary pressure higher than atmospheric pressure would instead expel air.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The descriptions of diaphragm and external intercostal muscle contractions causing dimensional increases are true, whereas the claim that intra-pulmonary pressure rises above atmospheric pressure to cause inspiration is false.

answer.text: Statements I and II are correct, but Statement III is incorrect
Statements I and III are correct, but Statement II is incorrect
Statements II and III are correct, but Statement I is incorrect
Statements I, II and III are all correct

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER14_STATEMENT3_Q05 - Expiration mechanics and respiratory assessment parameters

questiontext.text:
Identify whether the following statements are correct or incorrect:

Statement I: Relaxation of the diaphragm and intercostal muscles returns them to their original positions, reducing thoracic volume and raising intra-pulmonary pressure slightly above atmospheric levels.

Statement II: Humans possess the ability to increase the strength of inspiration and expiration with the help of additional muscles in the abdomen.

Statement III: On average, a healthy adult human breathes 72 times per minute under resting conditions.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Quiet expiration is predominantly a passive process involving elastic recoil and relaxation of inspiratory muscles, while forceful expiration recruits accessory abdominal musculature. Physiological parameters establish standard baseline frequencies in healthy adults.

Step 2: Evaluation of First Proposition
Relaxation of the diaphragm allows it to arch upward, and relaxation of external intercostals lets the rib cage descend; this reduces both thoracic and pulmonary volumes, elevating intra-pulmonary pressure above atmospheric pressure to expel air.

Step 3: Evaluation of Second Proposition
Contraction of accessory muscles, particularly abdominal muscles and internal intercostals, increases intra-abdominal and intra-thoracic pressures to facilitate forced expiration and deeper inspiration.

Step 4: Evaluation of Third Proposition
A healthy resting human breathes at an average rate of 12 to 16 times per minute. The value of approximately 72 per minute represents the typical resting heart rate, not the respiratory rate.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The explanations of muscular relaxation during expiration and the recruitment of abdominal muscles are accurate, while the stated breathing rate of 72 breaths per minute is biologically incorrect.

answer.text: Statements I and II are correct, but Statement III is incorrect
Statements I and III are correct, but Statement II is incorrect
Statements II and III are correct, but Statement I is incorrect
Statements I, II and III are all correct

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER14_STATEMENT3_Q06 - Normal pulmonary volumes in human spirometry

questiontext.text:
Identify whether the following statements are correct or incorrect:

Statement I: Tidal volume (TV) is approximately 500 mL, corresponding to an inspiratory or expiratory volume of about 6000 to 8000 mL of air per minute in a healthy individual.

Statement II: Inspiratory reserve volume (IRV) represents the additional volume of air a person can inspire by forcible inspiration, averaging 2500 mL to 3000 mL.

Statement III: Expiratory reserve volume (ERV) averages 1100 mL to 1200 mL, which equals the volume remaining in the lungs after forcible expiration.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Standard lung volumes represent distinct anatomical and functional subdivisions of pulmonary air capacity measurable under resting or forced conditions.

Step 2: Evaluation of First Proposition
Normal quiet respiration moves roughly 500 mL of air per breath. At a breathing rate of 12 to 16 breaths per minute, the minute ventilation evaluates to \(500 \times 12 = 6000\text{ mL}\) to \(500 \times 16 = 8000\text{ mL}\) per minute.

Step 3: Evaluation of Second Proposition
The maximum extra volume that can be inhaled beyond normal tidal inspiration is the inspiratory reserve volume, with a physiological average range of 2500 to 3000 mL.

Step 4: Evaluation of Third Proposition
Expiratory reserve volume (ERV) is the extra volume expired forcibly after normal expiration, averaging 1000 to 1100 mL. The volume of air remaining in the lungs after a forcible expiration is the residual volume (RV), which averages 1100 to 1200 mL.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The values and descriptions for tidal volume and inspiratory reserve volume are accurate, whereas the statement conflates expiratory reserve volume with residual volume.

answer.text: Statements I and II are correct, but Statement III is incorrect
Statements I and III are correct, but Statement II is incorrect
Statements II and III are correct, but Statement I is incorrect
Statements I, II and III are all correct

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER14_STATEMENT3_Q07 - Clinical pulmonary capacities and mathematical relationships

questiontext.text:
Identify whether the following statements are correct or incorrect:

Statement I: Functional residual capacity (FRC) is the volume of air that remains in the lungs after a normal expiration and equals ERV + RV.

Statement II: Vital capacity (VC) is the maximum volume of air a person can breathe in after a forced expiration, which includes ERV, TV, and IRV.

Statement III: Total lung capacity (TLC) excludes residual volume because residual volume cannot be measured by a standard spirometer.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Pulmonary capacities represent combinations of two or more pulmonary volumes derived to assess pulmonary status and diagnose respiratory dysfunctions.

Step 2: Evaluation of First Proposition
After a standard, unforced exhalation, the air left behind in the respiratory tree consists of the expiratory reserve volume together with the residual volume, giving the equation \(\text{FRC} = \text{ERV} + \text{RV}\).

Step 3: Evaluation of Second Proposition
Vital capacity defines the greatest volume of air that can be expired following maximal inspiration (or inspired following maximal forced expiration), comprising \(\text{ERV} + \text{TV} + \text{IRV}\).

Step 4: Evaluation of Third Proposition
Total lung capacity is the entire volume of gas contained within the respiratory system following maximal inspiratory effort, explicitly defined as \(\text{TLC} = \text{VC} + \text{RV}\) (or \(\text{IRV} + \text{TV} + \text{ERV} + \text{RV}\)). Even though residual volume cannot be expired into a spirometer, it is inherently included in total lung capacity.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The definitions of functional residual capacity and vital capacity are correct, whereas the definition claiming total lung capacity excludes residual volume is incorrect.

answer.text: Statements I and II are correct, but Statement III is incorrect
Statements I and III are correct, but Statement II is incorrect
Statements II and III are correct, but Statement I is incorrect
Statements I, II and III are all correct

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER14_STATEMENT3_Q08 - Diffusion gradients and gas solubility dynamics

questiontext.text:
Identify whether the following statements are correct or incorrect:

Statement I: The partial pressure of oxygen (\(\text{pO}_2\)) in the alveoli is \(104\text{ mm Hg}\), while in deoxygenated blood arriving at the pulmonary capillaries it is \(40\text{ mm Hg}\).

Statement II: The solubility of carbon dioxide in blood is 20 to 25 times higher than that of oxygen.

Statement III: Because the partial pressure gradient for carbon dioxide between tissues and blood (\(45\text{ mm Hg}\) to \(40\text{ mm Hg}\)) is much smaller than that for oxygen, the total amount of carbon dioxide diffusing through the membrane per unit time is lower than that of oxygen.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Fick's law of diffusion dictates that net gas diffusion across a biological membrane depends on the partial pressure gradient, membrane thickness, membrane surface area, and the solubility coefficient of the diffusing gas.

Step 2: Evaluation of First Proposition
Alveolar gas has a normal \(\text{pO}_2\) of \(104\text{ mm Hg}\), whereas systemic venous blood entering pulmonary capillaries has a \(\text{pO}_2\) of \(40\text{ mm Hg}\), providing a robust gradient of \(64\text{ mm Hg}\) driving oxygen into blood.

Step 3: Evaluation of Second Proposition
Carbon dioxide displays a solubility roughly 20 to 25 times greater than that of oxygen in plasma and aqueous media.

Step 4: Evaluation of Third Proposition
Due to its 20- to 25-fold higher solubility, carbon dioxide diffuses through the respiratory membrane extremely rapidly despite having a relatively narrow partial pressure gradient (\(45\text{ mm Hg}\) vs \(40\text{ mm Hg}\)). The amount of carbon dioxide diffusing per unit difference in partial pressure is substantially greater than that of oxygen, not less.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The established alveolar and venous \(\text{pO}_2\) values and the 20-25 times higher solubility of \(\text{CO}_2\) are verified facts, while the claim that \(\text{CO}_2\) diffusion is lower due to a smaller pressure gradient is biologically false.

answer.text: Statements I and II are correct, but Statement III is incorrect
Statements I and III are correct, but Statement II is incorrect
Statements II and III are correct, but Statement I is incorrect
Statements I, II and III are all correct

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER14_STATEMENT3_Q09 - Histology and dimensions of alveolar diffusion membrane

questiontext.text:
Identify whether the following statements are correct or incorrect:

Statement I: The diffusion membrane is composed of three major layers: the thin squamous epithelium of alveoli, the endothelium of alveolar capillaries, and the intervening basement substance.

Statement II: The basement substance consists of a thin basement membrane supporting the alveolar squamous epithelium and the basement membrane surrounding the capillary endothelial cells.

Statement III: The total thickness of the diffusion membrane is approximately 2 to 3 millimetres, providing high mechanical strength to prevent capillary rupture.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Efficient gaseous exchange demands an exceptionally thin diffusion barrier to minimize resistance to the rapid diffusion of dissolved gases between the alveolar airspace and capillary erythrocytes.

Step 2: Evaluation of First Proposition
The anatomical respiratory membrane consists of the single-layered squamous epithelium forming the alveolar wall, the capillary endothelium, and the acellular basement substance located between them.

Step 3: Evaluation of Second Proposition
The intermediate basement layer is structurally composed of the basal lamina underlying the alveolar epithelium fused with the basal lamina surrounding the endothelial cells of the pulmonary capillary.

Step 4: Evaluation of Third Proposition
The entire thickness of the diffusion membrane is significantly less than one millimetre (typically fractions of a micrometre). A thickness of 2 to 3 millimetres would severely obstruct diffusion, resulting in immediate respiratory compromise.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The structural composition of the three layers and the nature of the basement substance are accurately presented, whereas the assertion that the diffusion membrane is several millimetres thick is false.

answer.text: Statements I and II are correct, but Statement III is incorrect
Statements I and III are correct, but Statement II is incorrect
Statements II and III are correct, but Statement I is incorrect
Statements I, II and III are all correct

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER14_STATEMENT3_Q10 - Hemoglobin stoichiometry and forms of blood oxygen transport

questiontext.text:
Identify whether the following statements are correct or incorrect:

Statement I: About 97 per cent of oxygen is transported by red blood cells in the blood, while the remaining 3 per cent is carried in a dissolved state through plasma.

Statement II: Haemoglobin is an iron-containing pigment present in red blood cells, and each haemoglobin molecule can bind reversibly with a maximum of four molecules of \(\text{O}_2\).

Statement III: A linear straight-line curve is obtained when the percentage saturation of haemoglobin with oxygen is plotted against \(\text{pO}_2\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Oxygen carriage depends on physical dissolution in aqueous plasma and reversible chemical association with the quaternary iron-porphyrin protein haemoglobin.

Step 2: Evaluation of First Proposition
Because oxygen exhibits low solubility in aqueous fluids, only 3% is dissolved in plasma, while 97% is transported bound to haemoglobin inside erythrocytes as oxyhaemoglobin.

Step 3: Evaluation of Second Proposition
Each haemoglobin tetramer contains four heme moieties containing ferrous (\(\text{Fe}^{2+}\)) ions, permitting each molecule to reversibly associate with up to four molecules of oxygen (\(\text{O}_2\)).

Step 4: Evaluation of Third Proposition
Because haemoglobin exhibits cooperative oxygen binding (allosteric subunit interactions), plotting percentage saturation against \(\text{pO}_2\) produces a sigmoid (S-shaped) curve, not a linear plot.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The physiological proportions of oxygen carriage and the four-molecule binding capacity of haemoglobin are correct, whereas the statement describing a linear oxygen dissociation curve is incorrect.

answer.text: Statements I and II are correct, but Statement III is incorrect
Statements I and III are correct, but Statement II is incorrect
Statements II and III are correct, but Statement I is incorrect
Statements I, II and III are all correct

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER14_STATEMENT3_Q11 - Environmental factors governing oxyhemoglobin formation and unloading

questiontext.text:
Identify whether the following statements are correct or incorrect:

Statement I: In the alveoli, high \(\text{pO}_2\), low \(\text{pCO}_2\), lesser \(\text{H}^+\) concentration, and lower temperature favour the formation of oxyhaemoglobin.

Statement II: In active tissues, low \(\text{pO}_2\), high \(\text{pCO}_2\), high \(\text{H}^+\) concentration, and higher temperature favour the dissociation of oxygen from oxyhaemoglobin.

Statement III: Under normal physiological conditions, every \(100\text{ mL}\) of oxygenated blood can deliver around \(15\text{ mL}\) of \(\text{O}_2\) to the tissues.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Binding of oxygen to haemoglobin is regulated by the partial pressure of oxygen and modulated by allosteric effectors including \(\text{pCO}_2\), acidity (\(\text{H}^+\)), and thermal energy, shifting the curve to facilitate pulmonary loading and peripheral unloading.

Step 2: Evaluation of First Proposition
At the alveolar interface, elevated \(\text{pO}_2\) coupled with minimal \(\text{pCO}_2\), reduced acidity (higher pH), and cooler temperature increases haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, maximizing oxyhaemoglobin loading.

Step 3: Evaluation of Second Proposition
At the metabolic tissue level, cellular catabolism generates \(\text{CO}_2\), lactic/carbonic acid, and heat while depleting oxygen; this microenvironment lowers oxygen affinity, stimulating efficient dissociation of oxygen.

Step 4: Evaluation of Third Proposition
Under resting physiological conditions, \(100\text{ mL}\) of arterial blood contains roughly \(19\) to \(20\text{ mL}\) of \(\text{O}_2\) and delivers approximately \(5\text{ mL}\) of \(\text{O}_2\) to systemic tissues, leaving venous blood approximately \(75\%\) saturated. A delivery of \(15\text{ mL}\) occurs only during extreme exercise, not normal resting physiology.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The conditions controlling oxyhaemoglobin association in the alveoli and dissociation in the tissues are accurate, while the claim of delivering \(15\text{ mL}\) of oxygen per \(100\text{ mL}\) of blood under normal conditions is incorrect.

answer.text: Statements I and II are correct, but Statement III is incorrect
Statements I and III are correct, but Statement II is incorrect
Statements II and III are correct, but Statement I is incorrect
Statements I, II and III are all correct

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER14_STATEMENT3_Q12 - Chemical forms and partitioning of carbon dioxide transport

questiontext.text:
Identify whether the following statements are correct or incorrect:

Statement I: Nearly 20 to 25 per cent of carbon dioxide is transported by RBCs as carbamino-haemoglobin.

Statement II: Nearly 70 per cent of carbon dioxide is transported as bicarbonate (\(\text{HCO}_3^-\)), facilitated by the enzyme carbonic anhydrase.

Statement III: About 7 per cent of carbon dioxide is carried in a dissolved state through plasma, while carbonic anhydrase is completely absent from blood plasma.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Carbon dioxide generated during cellular metabolism enters the bloodstream and is carried back to the pulmonary circulation in three distinct physical and chemical modes: dissolved in plasma, bound to haemoglobin amino groups, and converted to bicarbonate ions.

Step 2: Evaluation of First Proposition
Haemoglobin binds \(\text{CO}_2\) directly at its free amine terminals to form carbamino-haemoglobin, accounting for approximately 20 to 25 percent of the total blood transport.

Step 3: Evaluation of Second Proposition
The primary transport mechanism of \(\text{CO}_2\) is in the form of bicarbonate ions (\(\text{HCO}_3^-\)), representing roughly 70 percent of all transported carbon dioxide.

Step 4: Evaluation of Third Proposition
While about 7 percent of \(\text{CO}_2\) is transported physically dissolved in plasma, the metalloenzyme carbonic anhydrase is not completely absent from plasma; minute quantities exist in plasma, although its highest concentration is inside red blood cells.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The percentages attributed to carbamino-haemoglobin and bicarbonate transport are correct, but the claim that plasma lacks carbonic anhydrase entirely is inaccurate.

answer.text: Statements I and II are correct, but Statement III is incorrect
Statements I and III are correct, but Statement II is incorrect
Statements II and III are correct, but Statement I is incorrect
Statements I, II and III are all correct

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER14_STATEMENT3_Q13 - Carbonic anhydrase kinetics and peripheral carbon dioxide delivery

questiontext.text:
Identify whether the following statements are correct or incorrect:

Statement I: Carbonic anhydrase facilitates the reversible reaction: \(\text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_2\text{CO}_3 \rightleftharpoons \text{HCO}_3^- + \text{H}^+\) in both directions.

Statement II: At the alveolar site, where \(\text{pCO}_2\) is low, the carbonic anhydrase-mediated reaction proceeds toward the regeneration of \(\text{CO}_2\) and \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\).

Statement III: Every \(100\text{ mL}\) of deoxygenated blood delivers approximately \(4\text{ mL}\) of \(\text{CO}_2\) to the alveoli.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Bicarbonate equilibrium is driven by Le Chatelier's principle and the catalytic action of carbonic anhydrase responding to differing local partial pressures of carbon dioxide at the systemic tissues versus the pulmonary alveoli.

Step 2: Evaluation of First Proposition
Carbonic anhydrase catalyses both the forward hydration of carbon dioxide into carbonic acid (which dissociates into \(\text{HCO}_3^-\) and \(\text{H}^+\)) and its reverse dehydration into carbon dioxide and water.

Step 3: Evaluation of Second Proposition
In pulmonary capillary beds, alveolar \(\text{pCO}_2\) is relatively low (\(40\text{ mm Hg}\)), shifting the equilibrium toward the breakdown of bicarbonate and release of free \(\text{CO}_2\) gas across the respiratory membrane.

Step 4: Evaluation of Third Proposition
Under resting circulatory dynamics, venous blood passing through the pulmonary circulation discharges approximately \(4\text{ mL}\) of gaseous \(\text{CO}_2\) per \(100\text{ mL}\) into alveolar spaces for expiration.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
All three propositions accurately delineate the enzymatic reversibility of carbonic anhydrase, the direction of the reaction at pulmonary capillaries, and the exact quantity of carbon dioxide delivered per unit volume of blood.

answer.text: Statements I, II and III are all correct
Statements I and II are correct, but Statement III is incorrect
Statements I and III are correct, but Statement II is incorrect
Statements II and III are correct, but Statement I is incorrect

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER14_STATEMENT3_Q14 - Neural regulation centers and chemical respiratory sensitivity

questiontext.text:
Identify whether the following statements are correct or incorrect:

Statement I: A specialized respiratory rhythm centre in the medulla oblongata is primarily responsible for the neural regulation of respiration.

Statement II: The pneumotaxic centre in the pons region can transmit neural signals to reduce the duration of inspiration and thereby alter the respiratory rate.

Statement III: Oxygen concentration in arterial blood plays the primary, dominant role in regulating the respiratory rhythm centre, whereas \(\text{CO}_2\) and \(\text{H}^+\) ions have insignificant effects.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Breathing rhythmogenesis is mediated by autonomic centers within the brainstem (medulla and pons) and modulated via peripheral and central chemoreceptors sensitive to chemical alterations in internal body fluids.

Step 2: Evaluation of First Proposition
The primary respiratory rhythm centre resides in the medulla oblongata, producing rhythmic motor outputs to inspiratory and expiratory muscles to establish baseline ventilation.

Step 3: Evaluation of Second Proposition
The pneumotaxic centre, situated dorsally in the pons, acts as an 'off-switch' for inspiration: its neural impulses limit the duration of inspiration, leading to more frequent, shallower breaths.

Step 4: Evaluation of Third Proposition
The chemosensitive area in the medulla and peripheral chemoreceptors in the aortic arch and carotid arteries are extremely sensitive to fluctuations in \(\text{CO}_2\) and hydrogen ion concentration. The direct regulatory role of oxygen in regulating normal respiratory rhythm is quite insignificant.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The concepts identifying the medullary rhythm centre and the action of the pontine pneumotaxic centre are true, whereas the assertion that oxygen plays the primary regulatory role over carbon dioxide and hydrogen ions is completely reversed and false.

answer.text: Statements I and II are correct, but Statement III is incorrect
Statements I and III are correct, but Statement II is incorrect
Statements II and III are correct, but Statement I is incorrect
Statements I, II and III are all correct

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHING_AND_EXCHANGE_OF_GASES_STATEMENT_BASED_Q01 - Structural anatomy of the human respiratory system

questiontext.text:
Consider the following four statements regarding the anatomy of the human respiratory system:

(a) The trachea is a straight tube extending up to the mid-thoracic cavity, which divides at the level of the fifth thoracic vertebra into right and left primary bronchi.
(b) During swallowing, the glottis can be covered by a thin elastic cartilaginous flap called the epiglottis to prevent the entry of food into the larynx.
(c) The outer pleural membrane is in direct intimate contact with the lung surface, whereas the inner pleural membrane lines the thoracic cavity.
(d) Terminal bronchioles and alveolar sacs are supported by complete, rigid cartilaginous rings to keep the air passage permanently distended.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of tracheal division and cartilaginous support
The trachea extends through the neck into the mid-thoracic cavity and bifurcates at the level of the fifth thoracic vertebra into the right and left primary bronchi. Cartilaginous rings supporting the trachea, primary, secondary, and tertiary bronchi, and initial bronchioles are incomplete C-shaped rings; terminal bronchioles and alveoli completely lack cartilaginous rings.

Step 2: Evaluation of the epiglottis and sound box mechanism
The larynx is a cartilaginous box facilitating phonation. During deglutition, the opening to the larynx (glottis) is shielded by the epiglottis, an elastic cartilaginous flap, ensuring that ingested material is directed into the oesophagus rather than the respiratory tract.

Step 3: Evaluation of pleural membrane arrangement
The lungs are enclosed in a double-layered pleural sac. Anatomically, the outer pleural membrane lies in close contact with the thoracic wall lining, whereas the inner pleural membrane is directly adherent to the pulmonary surface.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Reviewing the anatomical facts confirms that the statements regarding the division of the trachea at the fifth thoracic vertebra and the protective closure by the epiglottis are factually correct, while the descriptions of pleural layer orientation and alveolar cartilaginous rings are incorrect.
Therefore, the correct evaluation includes only the statements concerning tracheal bifurcation at the fifth thoracic vertebra and epiglottic closure.

answer.text: (a) and (b) only
(b) and (c) only
(a) and (d) only
(c) and (d) only

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHING_AND_EXCHANGE_OF_GASES_STATEMENT_BASED_Q02 - Evaluation of pulmonary volumes and diagnostic capacities

questiontext.text:
Consider the following four statements regarding pulmonary volumes and capacities in a healthy human adult:

(a) Tidal volume is the volume of air inspired or expired during a normal respiration and amounts to approximately \(500\text{ mL}\).
(b) Inspiratory reserve volume is the volume of air remaining in the lungs after a normal expiration and averages \(1000\text{ mL}\) to \(1100\text{ mL}\).
(c) Functional residual capacity is the volume of air that remains in the lungs after a normal expiration, comprising expiratory reserve volume plus residual volume.
(d) Vital capacity is the volume of air remaining in the lungs even after a forcible expiration and averages \(1100\text{ mL}\) to \(1200\text{ mL}\).

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of resting ventilation volume
Tidal volume represents the volume inspired or expired in a relaxed, normal breath, measuring about \(500\text{ mL}\), translating to \(6000\text{ to }8000\text{ mL}\) of air per minute for a healthy individual.

Step 2: Evaluation of reserve volumes
Inspiratory reserve volume is the additional volume an individual can inhale by forced inspiration, averaging \(2500\text{ to }3000\text{ mL}\). The volume averaging \(1000\text{ to }1100\text{ mL}\) is the expiratory reserve volume, which is expired forcibly after a normal tidal expiration.

Step 3: Evaluation of pulmonary capacities
Functional residual capacity equals expiratory reserve volume plus residual volume, representing the air left in the lungs after a normal expiration. Vital capacity is the maximal volume that can be exhaled following a maximal inspiration (or inhaled after forced expiration), not the volume remaining after forced expiration (which defines residual volume, averaging \(1100\text{ to }1200\text{ mL}\)).

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The correct statements are precisely those defining tidal volume as approximately \(500\text{ mL}\) and functional residual capacity as the sum of expiratory reserve volume and residual volume.
Hence, the correct evaluation comprises the descriptions for tidal volume and functional residual capacity.

answer.text: (a) and (b) only
(a) and (c) only
(b) and (d) only
(c) and (d) only

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHING_AND_EXCHANGE_OF_GASES_STATEMENT_BASED_Q03 - Muscular mechanisms during inspiration and expiration phases

questiontext.text:
Consider the following four statements regarding the biomechanical mechanism of pulmonary ventilation in humans:

(a) Inspiration is initiated by the contraction of the diaphragm, which increases the volume of the thoracic cavity in the antero-posterior axis.
(b) Contraction of the external intercostal muscles lifts the ribs and sternum, increasing the thoracic chamber volume in the dorso-ventral axis.
(c) The increase in pulmonary volume causes intra-pulmonary pressure to rise above atmospheric pressure, forcing atmospheric air into the lungs.
(d) Normal quiet expiration is an active process initiated by the forceful contraction of abdominal muscles and internal intercostal muscles.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of the inspiratory diaphragm action
Contraction of the dome-shaped diaphragm flattens it downward, which increases the thoracic cavity dimensions along the antero-posterior axis.

Step 2: Evaluation of intercostal muscle activity in inspiration
Contraction of the external intercostal muscles elevates the ribs and the sternum upward and outward, thereby increasing the volume of the thoracic chamber in the dorso-ventral axis.

Step 3: Evaluation of pressure gradients in ventilation
The resultant total increase in thoracic volume induces an identical expansion of pulmonary volume. Boyle's law relationship dictates that pulmonary expansion decreases intra-pulmonary pressure to negative values relative to atmospheric pressure, creating a gradient that pulls air inward. Quiet expiration is primarily passive, caused by relaxation of the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles, whereas abdominal muscles are recruited only to augment forced expiration.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The statements accurately identifying the antero-posterior thoracic expansion via diaphragmatic contraction and dorso-ventral expansion via external intercostal contraction are true, while those proposing a positive pressure gradient for inspiration and active muscular contraction for quiet expiration are false.
Thus, the correct statements are those describing the directional expansions driven by the diaphragm and external intercostals.

answer.text: (b) and (c) only
(a) and (d) only
(a) and (b) only
(a), (c), and (d) only

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHING_AND_EXCHANGE_OF_GASES_STATEMENT_BASED_Q04 - Partial pressure gradients across human diffusion membranes

questiontext.text:
Consider the following four statements concerning the exchange of respiratory gases and partial pressures:

(a) The solubility of \(\text{CO}_2\) is \(20\text{ to }25\) times higher than that of \(\text{O}_2\), facilitating rapid diffusion across the respiratory surface.
(b) The diffusion membrane is composed of four distinct cellular layers whose cumulative thickness exceeds \(1.5\text{ mm}\).
(c) The partial pressure of carbon dioxide in deoxygenated blood is \(45\text{ mm Hg}\), which is identical to that found in metabolizing tissues.
(d) The partial pressure of oxygen in oxygenated blood entering systemic capillaries is \(104\text{ mm Hg}\), identical to alveolar air.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of relative gas solubility
Carbon dioxide exhibits a solubility coefficient \(20\text{ to }25\) times greater than that of oxygen, enabling equivalent or superior diffusion rates despite a much narrower partial pressure gradient across the respiratory membrane.

Step 2: Evaluation of the diffusion membrane histology
The respiratory diffusion barrier consists of three major components: the single-cell squamous epithelium of the alveolus, the capillary endothelium, and the non-cellular intervening basement substance. The entire barrier has a thickness much less than one millimetre (\(\ll 1\text{ mm}\)).

Step 3: Evaluation of physiological partial pressures
In tissues and systemic deoxygenated blood, \(p\text{CO}_2\) is \(45\text{ mm Hg}\), creating a gradient toward alveolar air (\(40\text{ mm Hg}\)). Meanwhile, \(p\text{O}_2\) in alveolar air is \(104\text{ mm Hg}\), whereas in systemic arterial oxygenated blood it equilibrates to \(95\text{ mm Hg}\), not \(104\text{ mm Hg}\).

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Statements detailing the higher solubility of carbon dioxide and the identical \(p\text{CO}_2\) value of \(45\text{ mm Hg}\) in deoxygenated blood and tissues are valid, whereas the statements detailing membrane thickness and arterial \(p\text{O}_2\) are erroneous.
Hence, the correct option comprises the statements concerning carbon dioxide solubility and partial pressure in deoxygenated blood.

answer.text: (a) and (d) only
(b) and (c) only
(b) and (d) only
(a) and (c) only

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHING_AND_EXCHANGE_OF_GASES_STATEMENT_BASED_Q05 - Physiochemical pathways of carbon dioxide transport blood

questiontext.text:
Consider the following four statements regarding the biochemical mechanisms of carbon dioxide transport in human blood:

(a) Approximately \(70\%\) of carbon dioxide is transported in blood plasma in the form of bicarbonate ions (\(\text{HCO}_3^-\)).
(b) About \(20\text{ to }25\%\) of carbon dioxide binds directly to the amino groups of haemoglobin to form carbamino-haemoglobin.
(c) The enzyme carbonic anhydrase is present in extremely high concentrations in erythrocytes and is entirely absent from the blood plasma.
(d) Every \(100\text{ mL}\) of deoxygenated blood delivers approximately \(5\text{ mL}\) of carbon dioxide to the alveolar air.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of carbon dioxide transport fractions
Carbon dioxide is carried via three primary modes: roughly \(7\%\) in simple physical solution within plasma, \(20\text{ to }25\%\) chemically combined with haemoglobin as carbamino-haemoglobin, and approximately \(70\%\) as bicarbonate ions.

Step 2: Evaluation of carbonic anhydrase distribution
Erythrocytes contain a very high concentration of carbonic anhydrase, which rapidly catalyses the interconversion between \(\text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}\) and \(\text{HCO}_3^- + \text{H}^+\). However, the enzyme is not completely absent from plasma; minute quantities exist in blood plasma as well.

Step 3: Evaluation of delivered gas volumes
Under resting physiological conditions, every \(100\text{ mL}\) of deoxygenated blood releases approximately \(4\text{ mL}\) of \(\text{CO}_2\) to the alveoli. The quantity of \(5\text{ mL}\) per \(100\text{ mL}\) pertains to oxygen delivered by oxygenated blood to peripheral tissues.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
